Problem Addressed: Staff in sensitive roles can be induced by fraudulent recruitment processes to run attacker code on corporate endpoints; the September 2026 fake interview succeeded against a wallet-team engineer.
Recommended Solution: Mandate a recruitment-approach protocol: independent verification callback for any recruitment contact, and execution of all externally supplied code only inside managed sandbox environments with no production credentials or network reach.
Implementation Steps: 1) Issue interim directive to all engineering staff; 2) stand up sandbox VM image and block external-code execution outside it; 3) open a logged reporting channel for recruitment approaches; 4) brief wallet/signing teams first.
Dependencies: Sandbox infrastructure; HR/Legal concurrence on approach logging
Success Criteria: 100% of engineering staff acknowledged the directive; sandbox live; zero external-code executions on endpoints after go-live (EDR-verified).
Evidence of Completion: Directive and acknowledgement records; sandbox build records; EDR execution reports; approach log.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-01 likelihood reduced; provides the human-layer control whose absence enabled initial access.

Problem Addressed: Tampered installers (June 2026) and a trojanised component of a legitimate tool (September 2026) executed on engineering endpoints; endpoint tooling missed the September malware.
Recommended Solution: Enforce allow-listed, signature/hash-verified software installation on all engineering endpoints; block unmanaged installs; attest EDR coverage and health for 100% of the engineering estate, wallet teams first.
Implementation Steps: 1) Freeze non-essential installs on wallet/signing endpoints; 2) deploy allow-list enforcement with package-source pinning; 3) reconcile EDR enrolment to the engineering asset register; 4) clear or quarantine every exception.
Dependencies: Endpoint management platform capacity; change freeze windows
Success Criteria: Unmanaged install attempts blocked in testing and in production telemetry; EDR coverage 100% for wallet/signing stratum.
Evidence of Completion: Allow-list configuration exports; EDR coverage dashboards; blocked-install logs; exception register (empty or fully approved).
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-02 likelihood and R-03 exposure materially reduced; converts two historical bypasses into blocked events.

Problem Addressed: The detected and remediated June 2026 compromise still yielded the targeting intelligence (roles, team identities) for the successful September attack; remediation closed the device issue but not the exposure it created.
Recommended Solution: Create a post-compromise exposure protocol: every detected endpoint compromise triggers a documented exposure review (identities, roles, tokens and access reachable), credential rotation beyond the device, and 12 months of enhanced monitoring of the exposed individuals and their teams.
Implementation Steps: 1) Define trigger criteria and review template; 2) apply retrospectively to the June 2026 case for lessons; 3) integrate with the incident-response ticketing system; 4) assign ownership to Detection & Response.
Dependencies: IR process change approval; HR/privacy review of enhanced monitoring
Success Criteria: Protocol live; 100% of qualifying compromises receive a documented exposure review within 10 business days.
Evidence of Completion: Protocol document; completed exposure reviews; monitoring rule records.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-04 residual reduced: a detected compromise can no longer silently seed a follow-on targeted attack.

Problem Addressed: A long-lived container-deployment token stored on an engineer's laptop gave the attackers their production path on 29 October 2026.
Recommended Solution: Eliminate standing credentials from endpoints: discover and revoke endpoint-resident tokens; move deployment authority to a brokered, just-in-time, short-lived, single-purpose issuance model with full logging.
Implementation Steps: 1) Scan all engineering endpoints for token/key material; 2) revoke and rotate everything found; 3) enforce brokered issuance for deployment paths; 4) add continuous discovery scanning.
Dependencies: Token broker/vault readiness; deployment pipeline changes
Success Criteria: Zero deployment-capable tokens resident on endpoints (scan-verified); 100% of deployments traceable to brokered issuance.
Evidence of Completion: Discovery scan reports; revocation records; broker issuance logs; pipeline configuration.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-05 impact sharply reduced: a compromised laptop no longer carries production authority.

Problem Addressed: The signing service produced signatures with no corresponding approved withdrawal, and 50 EIP-7702 authorisations were created without any alert firing; detection of the theft was public before it was demonstrably internal.
Recommended Solution: Deploy signing-output invariant monitoring: real-time alerting on any signing event without a matching approved withdrawal (unmatched-signing alert) and on ANY EIP-7702 delegation involving treasury/hot wallets, with automatic suspension of signing for the affected wallet tier at defined thresholds.
Implementation Steps: 1) Instrument signing-service telemetry into the SIEM; 2) build the unmatched-signing correlation rule; 3) alert on any treasury-wallet delegation event; 4) wire automatic signing suspension for the affected tier at the Section 10 thresholds; 5) replay the 29 Oct event pattern as a test case.
Dependencies: Signing-service logging completeness; SIEM capacity; pre-authorised suspension authority (see REC-06)
Success Criteria: Test replay of the 29 Oct pattern generates alerts within 5 minutes and suspends the affected tier automatically; zero unalerted delegations in production.
Evidence of Completion: Rule definitions; replay test records; alert and suspension logs; threshold configuration.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-10 detection gap closed for the realised scenario; R-07 blast radius bounded by automatic suspension.

Problem Addressed: Revoking the malicious EIP-7702 delegations took until 00:10 UTC — about 3 hours 50 minutes after the delegation transaction — because MPC signing meant no single key could revoke and a specialised procedure had to be designed mid-incident; re-sweeps continued in the interval.
Recommended Solution: Establish a pre-tested revocation capability: documented and pre-approved revocation-signing methods for delegations and authorisations on every supported chain, MPC quorum pre-staging with a 24x7 on-call rota, and timed revocation drills with a target of full revocation within 30 minutes.
Implementation Steps: 1) Document revocation methods per chain; 2) pre-stage quorum availability (rota, contact tree, signing environment); 3) run the first timed live drill; 4) set the drill cadence at quarterly.
Dependencies: MPC provider/ceremony constraints; legal pre-approval of emergency signing
Success Criteria: Drill-measured time-to-revoke of under 30 minutes, evidenced twice before Phase 2 ends.
Evidence of Completion: Revocation runbooks; drill reports with timestamps; rota records.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-09 reduced from hours to minutes; containment no longer waits on procedure design.

Problem Addressed: Attackers moved from a compromised endpoint to peer machines via internal tooling and onward to the signing service; the actual reachability of the signing environment from corporate endpoints has never been publicly explained and must be assumed excessive.
Recommended Solution: Enforce deny-by-default segmentation: signing infrastructure reachable only via hardened, individually approved access paths; remove standing cross-endpoint action capability from internal tools (including AI tools) or place it behind per-action approval with full action logging.
Implementation Steps: 1) Map actual reachability (not documented topology); 2) close every unregistered path; 3) implement approved jump-path access with per-request approval; 4) re-scope internal tool identities to least privilege with logged, approved actions.
Dependencies: REC-04 (identity clean-up); change windows for production network policy
Success Criteria: Independent path-testing shows no route from a standard corporate endpoint profile to signing interfaces; all cross-endpoint tool actions are approved and logged.
Evidence of Completion: Rule exports; reachability test reports; tool permission matrices and action logs.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-06 reduced: endpoint compromise no longer implies signing-service reachability.

Problem Addressed: The signer would sign what an authorised caller sent; policy did not bind signatures to approved withdrawal parameters, and unexpected EIP-7702 authorisations were not rejected.
Recommended Solution: Implement a signing policy engine: per-chain, per-tier policies binding every signature to an approved withdrawal or policy envelope (destination allow-lists, per-transaction and velocity value caps); reject unexpected EIP-7702 authorisations by default; dual approval above value thresholds.
Implementation Steps: 1) Define policy schema per wallet tier and chain; 2) integrate policy checks into the signing path (fail-closed); 3) default-deny delegation creation outside a change process; 4) back-test policy against the 29 Oct event pattern.
Dependencies: REC-05 telemetry; signing-service release train
Success Criteria: Back-test shows the 29 Oct signature requests rejected or escalated; zero policy-bypass paths in penetration and audit testing.
Evidence of Completion: Policy configurations; back-test and penetration-test reports; signing decision logs.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-07 reduced: valid credentials alone can no longer produce arbitrary signatures.

Problem Addressed: Approximately $6.34B-$6.43B was held where a signing compromise could reach it; hot-wallet exposure had no publicly evidenced limit, while a major peer publicly reports over 99% of assets in cold storage.
Recommended Solution: Adopt a board-approved hot-wallet exposure framework: maximum hot-wallet share of reserves per asset and chain, automated sweeping to cold storage above the cap, and daily exposure reporting to Treasury and Risk.
Implementation Steps: 1) Inventory hot-wallet balances by asset/chain; 2) set caps through the Risk Committee; 3) automate sweep logic and alerting on cap breach; 4) report exposure daily.
Dependencies: Cold-storage capacity and signing ceremony throughput; Risk Committee approval
Success Criteria: Hot-wallet share at or below cap for 30 consecutive days; zero unexplained cap breaches.
Evidence of Completion: Exposure reports; sweep logs; Risk Committee minutes approving caps.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-08 impact capped: a repeat signing compromise cannot reach the full reserve.

Problem Addressed: Containment of the freezable share depended on ad hoc, if fast, coordination with issuers (freezes from 21:01 UTC) and authorities; about $3.0B in non-issuer-controlled assets was never freezable at all.
Recommended Solution: Formalise a freeze-coordination framework: pre-authorised freeze-request packages for major issuers and venues, 24x7 escalation contacts, pre-agreed evidentiary formats, and joint tabletop exercises; maintain the FBI/authority address-list screening as a standing control.
Implementation Steps: 1) Draft freeze-request packages per major issuer; 2) establish and test contact trees; 3) run a joint tabletop; 4) set a dispatch target of 15 minutes from confirmed theft.
Dependencies: Issuer/legal agreements; law-enforcement liaison arrangements
Success Criteria: Tabletop demonstrates freeze requests dispatched within 15 minutes with complete evidentiary packages.
Evidence of Completion: Package templates; contact-tree test records; exercise reports.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-11 residual reduced for the freezable share; the unfreezable share is addressed only by REC-09 exposure caps, and the register says so.

Problem Addressed: Proof-of-reserves assurance weakened during the incident itself: the 4 November snapshot's ZK proof has no announced completion, and the 12 November 198-token proof was pending at announcement; a snapshot without its proof is an assertion, not a verification.
Recommended Solution: Create a PoR integrity programme: fixed snapshot cadence; every snapshot tracked to proof publication as a controlled deliverable with escalation to the CFO and Audit Committee if a proof is not published within its stated window; publish a roadmap toward liabilities-inclusive assurance.
Implementation Steps: 1) Register all snapshots and proof deadlines in a control calendar; 2) assign proof-delivery ownership; 3) define the escalation path for a missed window; 4) publish the assurance roadmap.
Dependencies: ZK proving capacity at expanded token counts; external assurance providers
Success Criteria: 100% of snapshots have proofs published within their stated windows for two consecutive cycles; any miss escalated and publicly explained.
Evidence of Completion: Control calendar; proof publication records; escalation records.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-13 reduced: reserve claims become verifiable on schedule, or visibly late.

Problem Addressed: Public figures conflicted during the incident: coverage was announced at 90% on 31 Oct and restated as 98% for the same date on 3 Nov; acknowledgement times differ across timelines; outflow figures were published for overlapping windows that cannot be reconciled.
Recommended Solution: Implement disclosure control for incidents: a single-source-of-truth figures log (value, definition, source system, timestamp, owner) behind every public number; dual sign-off (Finance + Legal/Comms) before publication; a standing correction protocol that issues corrections as prominently as the original figure.
Implementation Steps: 1) Build the figures-log template and workflow; 2) assign figure owners; 3) apply retrospectively to this incident's published figures and issue any needed corrections; 4) train spokespeople on the log.
Dependencies: Legal review; Finance data owners
Success Criteria: Zero public incident figures published without a log entry; the 31 Oct coverage discrepancy publicly reconciled or corrected.
Evidence of Completion: Figures log; sign-off records; published correction (if required).
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-15 reduced: disclosure becomes an auditable control rather than a narrative risk.

Problem Addressed: Endpoint and signing detection both failed silently in the realised attack; detection capability is currently asserted, not measured.
Recommended Solution: Build a detection-measurement programme: behavioural analytics over signing and endpoint telemetry, detection-time metrics for real and simulated events, and recurring purple-team exercises replaying the endpoint-to-signing attack path.
Implementation Steps: 1) Define detection metrics and targets; 2) instrument the full attack path; 3) run the first purple-team replay; 4) report metrics quarterly to the Risk Committee.
Dependencies: REC-05 and REC-07 telemetry/segmentation in place
Success Criteria: Simulated attack path detected at or before the signing stage in exercise; detection-time metrics produced for two consecutive quarters.
Evidence of Completion: Analytics rule inventory; exercise reports; metrics dashboards.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-03 and R-10 residuals reduced on measured, not asserted, performance.

Problem Addressed: Wallet and signing engineers are identifiable, high-value targets for state-level social engineering; targeting risk is currently managed, if at all, as a general awareness topic.
Recommended Solution: Establish a personnel-security programme for high-risk roles: role-based targeting risk assessments, enhanced verification and reporting support for external approaches, platform-profile guidance, and periodic targeted simulations.
Implementation Steps: 1) Complete targeting risk assessments for wallet/signing/infrastructure roles; 2) issue role-specific guidance; 3) run targeted simulations; 4) review quarterly with HR and Legal.
Dependencies: HR/Legal partnership; privacy review
Success Criteria: 100% of high-risk roles assessed; simulation report rate at or above 90%; guidance adopted by all in-scope teams.
Evidence of Completion: Risk assessments; guidance documents; simulation reports.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-01/R-02 reduced for the population the adversary actually targets.

Problem Addressed: Coverage of a $6.34B+ loss was assembled during the incident from three sources whose final allocation remains undisclosed; SAFU's refill to ~$1B is promised but unconfirmed; no documented coverage policy sized for a signing-compromise stress case has been evidenced.
Recommended Solution: Adopt and publish internally a coverage and reserve policy: sizing methodology including a signing-compromise stress scenario, funding-source hierarchy, decision authority, refill triggers and deadlines for SAFU-class reserves, and quarterly board reporting on reserve adequacy.
Implementation Steps: 1) Model stress scenarios with Finance/Risk; 2) draft the policy and funding hierarchy; 3) obtain Board Risk Committee approval; 4) produce the final allocation report for this incident and confirm SAFU refill status.
Dependencies: Board Risk Committee approval; actuarial/risk modelling input
Success Criteria: Policy approved and in force; final incident allocation reported to the Board; SAFU refill confirmed by evidence, not announcement.
Evidence of Completion: Approved policy; allocation report; reserve balance evidence; committee minutes.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-12 reduced: the next loss of this class is pre-funded by policy, not improvised.

Problem Addressed: Withdrawal suspension protected the platform but imposed ~2.5 days without withdrawals and phased access beyond day 14, with reopening executed as a manual, batch-by-batch programme.
Recommended Solution: Engineer withdrawal resilience: granular per-network/per-asset pause and reopen capability, pre-defined reopening criteria, surge-capacity testing for reopening demand, and pre-approved customer communication templates for each phase.
Implementation Steps: 1) Build granular pause/reopen controls; 2) define and approve reopening criteria; 3) load-test reopening surges; 4) approve communication templates with Legal/Comms.
Dependencies: Core trading/wallet platform release capacity
Success Criteria: Game-day demonstrates a full pause-and-phased-reopen cycle inside target times with criteria applied as documented.
Evidence of Completion: Engineering deliverables; game-day reports; approved criteria and templates.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-14 reduced: containment can be surgical and recovery predictable.

Problem Addressed: The incident's regulatory position is fragmented: no single US federal cyber regime for exchanges, state regimes of very different depth (NYDFS the most prescriptive), no non-US regulator statement located, and sanctions/AML dimensions driven by a state attribution — with no maintained obligations picture evidenced.
Recommended Solution: Create a regulatory obligations and engagement programme for cyber incidents: a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction obligations register (reporting, examination, sanctions-screening, customer-notification), maintained by Legal/Compliance, with proactive regulator briefings after major incidents.
Implementation Steps: 1) Build the obligations register from licensed-entity mapping; 2) assign owners per jurisdiction; 3) brief key regulators on this incident and remediation; 4) review the register semi-annually.
Dependencies: Entity/licence mapping across the group; external counsel in key jurisdictions
Success Criteria: Register complete for all licensed jurisdictions; briefings delivered; register review evidenced.
Evidence of Completion: Obligations register; briefing records; review minutes.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-16 reduced: obligations are known before an incident tests them.

Problem Addressed: A single signing service covering every chain gave one intrusion the whole hot-wallet estate; segmentation and policy controls (REC-07/REC-08) mitigate but do not remove the architectural concentration.
Recommended Solution: Transform the signing architecture: segregated signing services and independent approval paths per chain and wallet tier, with value-scaled threshold approvals, so no single compromise domain can sign across the estate.
Implementation Steps: 1) Design target architecture with blast-radius limits per domain; 2) migrate chains in tranches; 3) decommission the unified signing path; 4) independently verify the final topology.
Dependencies: REC-07/REC-08 complete; migration windows per chain
Success Criteria: No single compromise domain can produce signatures for more than its own tier/chain set, verified by independent test.
Evidence of Completion: Architecture records; migration reports; independent verification report.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-06/R-07 structural residual reduced: blast radius is architectural, not procedural.

Problem Addressed: Reusable credentials and tokens were the connective tissue of the intrusion; brokered issuance (REC-04) covers deployment paths but privileged engineering access generally remains to be hardened.
Recommended Solution: Complete the identity transformation: phishing-resistant, hardware-backed authentication for all privileged engineering and production access; elimination of reusable credentials on production paths; continuous access review for signing-adjacent roles.
Implementation Steps: 1) Inventory privileged access paths; 2) roll out hardware-backed authentication; 3) remove reusable-credential fallbacks; 4) institute quarterly access reviews.
Dependencies: Hardware token logistics; legacy tooling replacement
Success Criteria: 100% of privileged production access via hardware-backed authentication; zero reusable credentials on production paths (scan/audit verified).
Evidence of Completion: Rollout records; access-review minutes; scan reports.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-05 residual reduced across all privileged paths, not only deployment.

Problem Addressed: Custody and coverage assurance currently rests on snapshots and announcements; nothing independent attests that the controls over signing and reserves operate over time.
Recommended Solution: Commission recurring independent assurance over custody and signing controls (SOC 2 Type II or agreed-upon procedures of equivalent rigour), including the coverage/reserve policy's operation, with a public summary cadence.
Implementation Steps: 1) Select the assurance framework and provider; 2) complete the first observation period; 3) publish the summary; 4) fix the recurring cycle.
Dependencies: REC-15 policy in force; control maturity from Phases 1-3
Success Criteria: First independent report issued with no unremediated critical exceptions; public summary published.
Evidence of Completion: Assurance report; published summary; exception remediation records.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-08/R-12 assurance gap closed: custody claims become independently attested.

Problem Addressed: The response's strengths (freeze speed, phased reopening) and weaknesses (revocation latency, disclosure conflicts) were improvised under pressure; without rehearsal they will not reliably recur.
Recommended Solution: Institutionalise an incident-resilience exercise programme: semi-annual signing-compromise exercises including timed revocation, issuer freeze coordination, coverage decision-making and disclosure under the figures-log discipline.
Implementation Steps: 1) Build the exercise scenario library from this incident; 2) run the first full exercise; 3) track corrective actions to closure; 4) report exercise outcomes to the Risk Committee.
Dependencies: Issuer participation for freeze tabletop; executive availability
Success Criteria: Two exercises completed in 12 months with all corrective actions closed or risk-accepted by the Risk Committee.
Evidence of Completion: Exercise reports; corrective-action tracker; committee minutes.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-04/R-14 reduced: response quality becomes a rehearsed capability.

Problem Addressed: This incident's transparency was comparatively fast — a preliminary report in five days — but the final post-mortem has no committed date, some details are withheld permanently, and figure discipline failed once; none of the good practice is yet a standard.
Recommended Solution: Adopt a public transparency standard: preliminary incident report within five business days of a major incident, a committed window for the final post-mortem, proof-publication service levels for reserve attestations, and the figures-log discipline (REC-12) as a permanent control.
Implementation Steps: 1) Draft the standard with Legal/Comms/Security; 2) obtain executive and Board approval; 3) publish the standard; 4) report compliance after every major incident.
Dependencies: Board approval; REC-11/REC-12 operating
Success Criteria: Standard published; compliance reported after the next major incident (and retrospectively assessed for this one).
Evidence of Completion: Published standard; compliance reports.
Expected Residual Risk Reduction: R-13/R-15 reduced durably: transparency survives personnel and pressure changes.
